summary: This informational document analyzes threats to Multipath TCP (MPTCP) that remain after the protocol's earlier security work, and explores possible solutions to address them.

eli5.summary: Multipath TCP lets one connection use several roads at once. This note asks what sneaky attacks are still possible and how to block them.

questions: what is the mptcp add_addr attack
how to prevent mptcp syn flooding
what are the residual threats for mptcp
subtitle: A second look at the security holes still left in Multipath TCP, and how to patch them.

tldr.problem: Multipath TCP (MPTCP) was designed so that it is no less secure than ordinary single-path TCP, but the protocol as written in RFC 6824 still allows several attacks that plain TCP does not.
tldr.mechanism: The document walks through five MPTCP-specific attacks (ADD_ADDR hijack, DoS on MP_JOIN, SYN flooding amplification, an eavesdropper in the initial handshake, and SYN/JOIN address substitution), says who can mount each one, and suggests fixes.
tldr.outcome: The authors recommend adding an HMAC to the ADD_ADDR option so that MPTCP could move to the Standards Track, and exploring tcpcrypt or SSL-based keys for stronger protection later.

today: RFC 7430 is an Informational document and the data does not list any RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It analyzes the Experimental MPTCP specification RFC 6824 as it stood in July 2015 and complements the earlier analysis in RFC 6181.

sections.title: Why a Second Threat Analysis
sections.content:
RFC 6181 was a threat analysis written before the MPTCP specification (RFC 6824) was finished. It looked at the general idea of letting TCP use several IP addresses per connection and fed recommendations into the design. This document complements it with a vulnerability analysis of the mechanisms RFC 6824 actually specifies.

The yardstick stays the same as in RFC 6824: MPTCP should be no worse than single-path TCP. So the document only covers threats that are specific to MPTCP and not possible with single-path TCP. Threats shared by TCP and MPTCP are left out.
sections.eli5: Before building a new bridge, engineers checked it for weak spots. Now that it is built, they check again, and this time only for weak spots that an ordinary road would not have.

sections.title: Kinds of Attackers
sections.content:
For every attack the document names the type of attacker. Attackers are classed by location: an off-path attacker never sees the session's packets, a partial-time on-path attacker is on at least one path for part of the session, and an on-path attacker is on at least one path for the whole session.

They are also classed by action: an eavesdropper can capture packets but not change, discard or delay them, while an active attacker can change, discard or delay some packets. The analysis uses five combinations: on-path eavesdropper, on-path active, off-path active, partial-time on-path eavesdropper and partial-time on-path active.
sections.eli5: Some troublemakers can only listen at the door, some can also grab and change notes, and some are never near the door at all. The note asks what each kind could do.

sections.title: The ADD_ADDR Hijack
sections.content:
This is the main attack, mounted by an off-path active attacker. Host A and Host B have an MPTCP session. Attacker Host C forges a packet that looks like it comes from A to B, with the ACK flag set and an ADD_ADDR option announcing C's address as an alternative address. B, if it is configured to start new subflows, answers with a SYN carrying MP_JOIN, the token of A and a random nonce. C rewrites the addresses and relays the handshake between A and B, so a new subflow now passes through C. To take over the whole session, C can also send TCP RST packets to both sides to kill the original subflow.

The attacker has to know or guess the four-tuple of the connection, a valid sequence number, a valid ACK number and an unused 8-bit address identifier. It must also be able to forge source addresses, so ingress filtering (RFC 2827) or source address validation (RFC 7039) in its network would stop it, although the text notes that ingress filtering is not as widely implemented as one would expect.

The document gives formulas for how many packets a blind attacker needs. Without RFC 5961, a 4000-port ephemeral range and a 16 KB window need up to 699050 packets at an MSS of 1500 bytes. With RFC 5961 support, the same case needs 45812984490 packets.

Three fixes are listed: put the connection token in ADD_ADDR, put an HMAC of the address in ADD_ADDR, or include the SYN destination address in the MP_JOIN HMAC. The third would stop hosts behind NATs from being reached through an advertised address. The HMAC option is recommended because it gives the highest security level while keeping NAT compatibility.
sections.eli5: A stranger sends a fake note saying "you can also reach me at my house," and then passes messages between the two friends without either noticing. Adding a secret stamp to that note stops the trick.

sections.title: Flooding the Join Handshake
sections.content:
The initial SYN+MP_JOIN of a new subflow carries a 32-bit token and a 32-bit random nonce. They are not repeated in the third ACK, so a host has to create state when the SYN arrives. An off-path attacker who knows (or guesses) the token can send many SYN+MP_JOIN packets with different 5-tuples until the per-session limit of half-open connections is used up. That stops the real peer from adding subflows.

The same weakness gives a SYN flooding amplification. Ordinary SYNs can be handled statelessly with SYN cookies, but SYN+MP_JOIN cannot. An attacker sends one regular SYN, which creates one piece of state, then sends as many SYN+MP_JOINs as the server supports. The server pays for all of them, while the attacker pays only for the first.

The proposed fix is to repeat the token and nonce in the third packet and let Host B derive its own nonce reproducibly (for example, a hash of the 5-tuple, the initial sequence number and a local secret), so it can answer without keeping state. Limiting half-open subflows to a low number, such as three, would also reduce the amplification.
sections.eli5: Imagine a receptionist who must write a note for every person who says "I'm with the group." A prankster says it a hundred times and the notepad fills up, so the real guests get turned away.

sections.title: Eavesdroppers and Address Substitution
sections.content:
Two further threats come from a partial-time on-path eavesdropper. The first is an eavesdropper present during the initial handshake, when the keys are exchanged. It learns the keys and can hijack the session at any time later, even after moving away from the path. The second is an attacker who sees the SYN/JOIN exchange and replaces the source address with one it chooses, so it can add any address it wants.

Both were identified when the MPTCP security solution was designed (RFC 6181), and the threat was judged acceptable at that time. For the first, possible enhancements are hash chains, SSL keys, Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGAs), tcpcrypt and DNSSEC. For the second, the document argues the weakness is fundamental because MPTCP must work through NATs, and NAT behavior is indistinguishable from this attack. Securing the address is therefore not an option, and protecting the payload (for example with tcpcrypt) looks more promising.
sections.eli5: If someone watches you swap secret passwords on day one, they can use them later. And if the mail passes through a post office that rewrites return addresses, you cannot trust the return address, so it is better to lock the letter itself.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
At the time of writing the MPTCP specification (RFC 6824) was Experimental, with work under way to move it to the Standards Track. The authors propose two threads of work. The first is to fix what is needed for Standards Track: the ADD_ADDR attack must be addressed by adding an HMAC to the ADD_ADDR message, using the address being added as input along with the key. That would make ADD_ADDR as secure as the JOIN message, and any better way to create the session key would improve both at once.

They argue this brings MPTCP to a security level similar to single-path TCP and equal to SCTP with dynamic addresses (RFC 5061), which relies on the authentication of RFC 4895. The second thread is exploring stronger designs, such as integration with tcpcrypt or SSL, because securing JOIN messages is fundamentally incompatible with NAT support. The document's own Security Considerations section says only that the whole document is about security considerations for MPTCP.
sections.eli5: The authors say: put a secret stamp on the new-address note and the bridge is safe enough to open to everyone. Later, look at ways to lock the cargo itself.
